mappings.note: Rare and expensive books. Extraction; the motive behind the collecting is a separate item.
Retrieves the once-a-year pattern and its reason. Extraction, not LO-4: no judgement of him is asked.
Identifies the lady in red as the speaker. Extraction at the point in the text where she is still taken for the mistress, so not C-E2.2-LO-9.
'Who is the real culprit' is LO-9's first clause word for word. Not LO-11: the item wants the identification, not the message.
Asks at what point the reader suspected her -- that is the 'how the writer withholds that fact until the close' half of LO-9.
The subtle deceptions and Horace's failure to suspect are misplaced trust with the woman in red as the illustration. Not LO-9: the culprit's identity is assumed, the technique is the question.
'Good and respectable but not completely honest' and 'not a typical thief' are both character judgements. Not C-E2.2-LO-10, which is about the fingerprints.
Where the meticulous planner went wrong is the removed gloves. LO-10 is exactly 'convicted by his own hands'.
Whether the punishment was fair turns on his being jailed for a theft he did not complete -- the irony LO-10 names. Not LO-8, which is about the proverb.
'Do intentions justify actions' generalises the writer's message beyond the plot. Not C-E2.2-LO-8: no saying is named, and not LO-11, since the woman in red is not the subject.
Names Victor Canning. Extraction.
His public reputation as good and honest -- the character the story then undercuts.
London. Extraction.
Books. Extraction.
The drawing room. Extraction.
Behind a painting. Extraction.
Completes the quoted thought with 'foolish'. Extraction of the wording.
The magazine article. Extraction.

Mapped as extraction about who addresses Horace. DEFECT: the key is 'sherry', the house dog, which cannot be right -- the short-answer item on the same question in this chapter is keyed 'the lady in red', and the dog does not speak.
His first impulse was to run. Extraction.
Her refusal to pretend she never saw him is the move that closes the trap. Not LO-1: the item exists because the refusal is tactical.
All three self-justifications together are his self-image. Character, not LO-2, since the writer does not endorse them.
Arrested on the third morning. Extraction of the event; the reason for it is the next item.
Fingerprints as the evidence: LO-10's 'convicted by his own hands', literally.
His account was called nonsense. Extraction.
What angers him is talk of honour among thieves -- the saying the story is built to test. LO-8, not LO-10.
Allergic to the smell of flowers. Extraction.
The servants were at the pictures. Extraction.
Keys on a hook. Extraction.
All three signals -- her confidence, her knowledge of the house, the dog's welcome -- are why the trust was misplaced. Not LO-1, since the key is 'all of them'.
The forgotten combination is her pretext for using him. LO-11's illustration, not a retrievable fact about the safe.
Assistant librarian in the prison. Extraction.
Taking the gloves off to light the lighter is the single act that convicts him. The core LO-10 item.
His success as a lock maker is the respectability the story sets against the theft. Character.
The flowers as the hindrance. Extraction.
Sherry is the dog. Extraction.
The threat to call the police is the lever she uses. Her method, so LO-11 rather than plain recall.
Shotover Grange. Extraction.
Rare and expensive books again, in MCQ form. Extraction.
That he was unmarried is part of the sketch of the solitary, respectable collector. Character.
Fifty years old. Extraction.
One safe a year. Extraction.
Three books coming up for sale. Extraction.
The thief claiming to protect 'society' is the woman in red's cover at its most brazen. Not LO-8: no proverb is quoted.
Drawing room, behind the painting. Extraction.

'A thief cheated by another thief' is the saying the story illustrates, which LO-8 asks to be stated and justified. DEFECT: the model answer names the betrayer as 'Mr. Cornelius', who is not in this story -- the deceiver is the woman in red.
She gets the jewels leaving no prints while his are everywhere: her deception and his self-conviction in one question.
The hobby and how he funded it. Both stated. Extraction.
Why he took her for the mistress -- the mechanics of the misplaced trust. Not LO-9, which is about the reveal.
The hay fever and the bowl of flowers. Extraction.
Her voice, her walk to the fireplace, her straightening the ornaments: the performance that earned the trust. LO-11.
The irony of 'society must be protected from men like you' is that the speaker is the real culprit. LO-9, not LO-10, which is about his fingerprints.
Asks the meaning of the saying itself. The clearest LO-8 item in the chapter.
Names the dog, locates the kitchen and retrieves his trick with dogs. All extraction.
Retrieves the passing thought about collecting pictures instead of books, and why he dropped it. Extraction.
Frequency plus what he did with the proceeds. Extraction.
Two weeks of study, the family away, the servants out. Extraction.
The fabricated story about the bank, the party and the forgotten numbers is her whole con. LO-11.
Arrested although he kept nothing, because his prints were everywhere. LO-10's irony stated as a question.
Why the phrase angers him: the saying failed him. LO-8, with the justification drawn from the events.
What he knew of the house -- rooms, wiring, paths, garden. Extraction.
Same ground as the earlier confidence item. Extraction.
The broken promise not to report him is the trust betrayed. LO-11, not LO-9: her identity is already known to the student here.
The real-culprit question at five marks: LO-9 for the substance, LO-3 for the extended answer with textual support.
Whether he was a threat to society and what qualities he lacks is a character verdict at length. Not LO-10: the fingerprints are not in question.
His fear of exposure and his failure to own the crime -- character, at five marks. Not LO-11: the lady is only the occasion.
'Describe how he planned the robbery' is retrieval assembled into a long answer. Not LO-10, which begins where the plan fails.
The lady as the better thief is both the saying about setting a thief to catch one and the misplaced-trust illustration, written at length.
Why he chose Shotover Grange: the fifteen thousand pounds of jewels, retrieved and written out.
Asks what such people should learn -- the writer's message carried outward. Not LO-4: Horace is treated as a type, not a portrait.
Built on his hope that her amusement meant sympathy, which is the misreading at the heart of LO-11, and asks what he should have understood about her.
Extract-based, and every sub-item is retrieval from the printed passage: the dog, the greeting, the tact, the location.

Sub-item i asks for an inference about Danby from his careful arranging of tools -- character -- alongside retrieval about the flowers. DEFECT: sub-item ii is keyed 'True because Horace knew the code', but the passage's reason is that he had lived with locks all his life, and he did not know the code.
